title: Faster Scientific Simulations with New FP64 Algorithms in NVIDIA cuBLAS | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA cuBLAS in CUDA Toolkit 13.4.2 adds Ozaki-II (CRT-based) and 2M complex-multiply algorithms that emulate full-accuracy FP64 GEMM on integer Tensor Cores, delivering 3.9x-5.5x DGEMM speedups on GB200/VR NVL72 and up to 23x on RTX PRO 6000. Validated end-to-end on CCSD quantum chemistry and BerkeleyGW, it signals NVIDIA's strategy of serving HPC double-precision demand through low-precision integer hardware rather than native FP64 units.

themes.theme: FP64 emulation on integer Tensor Cores

insights.claim: NVIDIA cuBLAS in CUDA Toolkit 13.4.2 computes double-precision GEMM by splitting FP64 numbers into integer pieces, multiplying them on integer Tensor Cores, and reassembling exact results, with no application code changes required.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: HPC buyers can get FP64 science throughput from AI-oriented GPUs, weakening the case for dedicated FP64 silicon and broadening NVIDIA's addressable HPC market.
insights.quote: With CUDA Toolkit 13.4.2, cuBLAS no longer has to choose between accuracy and speed.
insights.locator: With CUDA Toolkit 13.4.2, cuBLAS no longer

insights.claim: The Ozaki-II scheme uses the Chinese Remainder Theorem so integer GEMM count grows linearly with the number of moduli, versus quadratically with slice count for Ozaki-I, requiring roughly half as many Tensor Core GEMMs at FP64-equivalent accuracy.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: Algorithmic gains compound on existing hardware, so software releases alone can lift effective FP64 performance of installed NVIDIA fleets.
insights.quote: At the accuracy required to match FP64, Ozaki-I needs roughly twice as many Tensor Core GEMMs as Ozaki-II.
insights.locator: Ozaki-II uses a faster big-integer multiplication algorithm

insights.claim: cuBLAS's Automatic Dynamic Precision (ADP) framework falls back to native FP64 MMA instructions when the mantissa bits needed for FP64-equivalent accuracy exceed the default or user-set maximum, so emulation is positioned as safe for production.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: The accuracy safety net lowers adoption risk for conservative HPC users, accelerating migration of scientific codes onto emulated FP64.
insights.quote: So, applications can safely use cuBLAS in their production deployments without worrying about numerical accuracy.
insights.locator: cuBLAS ADP framework is designed to provide accuracy guarantees

insights.claim: cuBLAS applies the memory-parsimonious tiling introduced for Ozaki-I in CTK 13.3 to Ozaki-II, discarding each residue pair right after its GEMM to keep workspace manageable.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: Memory overhead is a key adoption barrier for emulation; solving it makes the technique viable on memory-constrained GPUs.
insights.locator: Because Ozaki-II materializes one residue pair per modulus

insights.claim: cuBLAS DGEMM with Ozaki-II runs 5.5x faster than native FP64 on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and 3.9x faster on NVIDIA GB200, and 2x faster than Ozaki-I on GB200.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: Rubin-generation systems show larger emulated-FP64 gains, supporting NVIDIA's pitch to supercomputing centers for VR NVL72 upgrades.

insights.claim: cuBLAS DGEMM with Ozaki-II reaches up to 175 TFLOPS on NVIDIA VR NVL72, 147 TFLOPS on NVIDIA GB200, and 37 TFLOPS on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: Effective FP64 TFLOPS figures on emulation can be compared against AMD/Intel native-FP64 parts when assessing HPC procurement competitiveness.

insights.claim: The ceiling on Ozaki-II speedup depends on a GPU's ratio of integer Tensor Core throughput to native FP64 units; on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, which has weak native FP64, DGEMM gains range from 10x at the smallest sizes to 23x at the largest.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: Cheaper workstation/server GPUs with minimal FP64 become credible for double-precision science, potentially cannibalizing or expanding NVIDIA's HPC SKU mix.
insights.quote: The upper-bound of the performance gain depends on how much integer Tensor Core throughput a GPU has relative to its native FP64 units
insights.locator: The upper-bound of the performance gain depends

insights.claim: On GB200, ADP dispatches small DGEMM shapes to native FP64 because Ozaki-II offers no advantage there, with gains rising steadily to 3.9x at the largest shapes measured.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: Benefits concentrate in large dense workloads; small-matrix HPC codes on data-center GPUs see little gain.
insights.locator: DGEMM performance on GB200, RTX PRO 6000

insights.claim: NVIDIA Rubin GPUs introduce a TI16 numeric format (12-bit sign-magnitude integer, range [-2047, +2047]) used via the tcgen05.mma instruction to accelerate Ozaki-I and Ozaki-II computations.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is now designing hardware formats specifically for FP64 emulation, signaling a long-term bet on emulation over native FP64 silicon.
insights.quote: Rubin introduces a new numeric format, TI16 (12-bit integer in sign-magnitude format with range of [-2047, +2047]), that is aptly suited for the acceleration of Ozaki scheme computations.

insights.claim: Because Ozaki-II turns additions, subtractions, and products into exact integer operations, the 2M algorithm computes a complex matrix product with two real GEMMs instead of four, making ZGEMM cost roughly twice a real GEMM rather than four times.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: Complex-valued workloads (materials science, electronic structure, signal processing) get an outsized speedup, broadening GPU appeal in those HPC niches.
insights.quote: The end result is that a ZGEMM now costs roughly twice a real GEMM of the same size instead of four times.

insights.claim: cuBLAS ZGEMM using the 2M algorithm with Ozaki-II achieves a 5x speedup over native Complex FP64 (CFP64) on NVIDIA GB200.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: Existing GB200 deployments get a large free performance uplift for complex-precision codes through a library update.

insights.claim: CCSD quantum chemistry using Ozaki-II DGEMM achieves 2x and 1.4x end-to-end speedups over native FP64 on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and NVIDIA GB200 at full FP64 precision, and 5x and 3.5x in a domain-specific mixed-precision mode.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: End-to-end gains are much smaller than kernel gains at full precision, so real-world HPC upside depends on users accepting tuned mixed precision.

insights.claim: Across GPU generations, Ozaki-II CCSD at guaranteed full FP64 precision delivers 4.7x total speedup on Rubin versus A100, rising to 11.5x with a fixed 32-mantissa-bit budget, with full-precision correlation-energy errors below 10-14 Eh.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: Generational upgrade economics for computational chemistry customers look compelling, supporting HPC refresh cycles toward Rubin.
insights.locator: Ozaki-II DGEMM with ESC guaranteeing full FP64 precision

insights.claim: On Rubin, frozen-core CCSD/cc-pVTZ for the uracil dimer with 32 mantissa bits reaches 173 TFLOPS end-to-end, with individual GEMMs as high as 368 TFLOPS and an average of 200 TFLOPS.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: Shows emulated precision can push quantum chemistry throughput into hundreds of TFLOPS on a single GPU.
insights.locator: On Rubin for uracil dimer frozen-core CCSD/cc-pVTZ

insights.claim: BerkeleyGW's Epsilon module using Ozaki-II 2M ZGEMM with 53 bits achieves 3.9x end-to-end speedup on GB200 and 6.6x on VR NVL72 over native ZGEMM, while matching Epsilon matrix elements to 10 decimal places per the NERSC-10 harness.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: Validation against the NERSC-10 harness ties the technique directly to a major upcoming US supercomputer procurement benchmark.

insights.claim: NVIDIA states GPUs give BerkeleyGW an 86x speedup over a CPU-only implementation, before the further cuBLAS ZGEMM enhancements.
insights.speaker: Cole Brower
insights.so_what: Reinforces the GPU-over-CPU narrative in scientific computing that underpins NVIDIA's HPC share.
insights.quote: Using GPUs with BerkeleyGW can lead to an 86x performance speedup over the CPU-only implementation
insights.locator: The BerkeleyGW code is used by researchers
